source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: Founding study. Three players (master M, Class A player A, beginner B) did two tasks on the same positions: a perception task (copy a board in plain view) and de Groot's 5 s memory task. Glances and pauses were used to cut the output into chunks.
numbers: N=3 players. 20 positions from games of masters, experts and a few Class A players: 10 middle game (about move 21, 24-26 pieces) and 10 end game (about move 41, 12-15 pieces). Random control positions use the same pieces.
quote: It is no mistake of language for the chess master to say that he sees the right move
limits: One subject per skill level, so no inferential skill effect. Source games weaker than de Groot's.
agent_relevance: The method turned a hidden thing (a chunk) into something countable: a time gap. Our agent could do the same for its own memory: log groupings and gaps in retrieval, not just answers.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: Recall depended on skill for real positions and not for random ones. After one 5 s view the master placed about 16 pieces right in middle-game positions, the class A player about 8, the beginner about 4. On random boards all three did worse than the beginner did on real boards.
numbers: Trial 1, middle game: M about 16, A about 8, B about 4 pieces. End game: M about 8, A about 7, B about 4. Nine tactical puzzle positions (5 s, one trial): B 33%, A 49%, M 81%, versus 18%, 34%, 62% on the first set. De Groot's masters placed 23-24 of 25 pieces. Random boards: no relation to skill.
limits: The master got about 16 of 25, well below de Groot's 23-24; the authors blame non-quiet positions and weaker source games. One subject per level. The random-position null was later disputed (see a18).
agent_relevance: Evidence that the gain is knowledge of the domain's own structure, not better general memory. For the agent: test any memory on shuffled or off-distribution items as a control.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: A surprising side result: recognizing the exact game did not help recall. The master recognized 4 of 9 puzzle positions within the first second, but recall was the same for recognized and unrecognized ones.
numbers: M recall 83% (recognized) vs 79% (not recognized). One earlier position recognized after trial 1 gave no gain on later trials.
limits: Tiny N (4 recognized positions, one subject). It is a hint, not a test.
agent_relevance: Whole-case matching may add little. What matters may be reuse of smaller parts. Do not assume an exact case match is the best cue.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: The 2 s boundary. In the copy task, pieces placed within one glance came fast and had many chess relations (defense, proximity, same colour, same type). Pieces placed after a glance back came slower and were related near chance. The memory task showed the same pattern with long pauses.
numbers: Within-glance gaps seldom over 2 s, modal gap half a second or less. About 2 s marks a chunk boundary. Correlation of relation profiles in the memory task: M vs A .91, M vs B .95, A vs B .95. Within-chunk relation frequencies were far from chance (large z); between-chunk frequencies were close to chance.
limits: The 2 s rule is a convention tested on 3 players and can include guessed pieces. Later work shows it depends on the apparatus (see a24).
agent_relevance: A cheap operational definition of a chunk (items produced with small gaps and many shared relations) could be applied to agent memory traces to measure how large its reusable units are.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: Chunk size and number. Chunks were small (about 2-4 pieces). Skill showed in the speed of perceiving a chunk and in the first few chunks. The master also recalled more chunks, which the theory had not expected.
numbers: Pieces per glance (middle game): 2.0 (M), 2.8 (A), 2.0 (B). Pieces per chunk in the memory task: 2.5, 2.1, 1.9. First recalled chunk: 3.8 (M), 2.6 (A), 2.4 (B). Chunks per trial, middle game: 7.7, 5.7, 5.3; end game: 7.6, 6.4, 4.2.
limits: The authors say the hypothesis of equal chunk number across skill was NOT supported and suspect the master reconstructs from general knowledge or organizes chunks above a flat list. This anomaly pushed the field toward templates.
agent_relevance: The reused unit is small (2-4 items) in this first account. A flat list of small items will not scale; some higher-level organization is needed.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: What the master's chunks contained. Over 75 percent were three familiar structures: pawn chains, castled-king positions, and clusters of same-colour pieces (back rank, connected rooks, queen with rooks). Attack chunks were also stereotyped.
numbers: 77 chunks (2+ pieces within 2 s) in 14 positions (5 middle game, 9 puzzle). 47 held a pawn chain. 27 were same-colour clusters (9 back-rank, 9 connected rooks or queen with rooks). 17 could not be classified. Of 18 strong attacks found by the authors, 11 were chunked.
limits: Classification done by the two authors, one master, 14 positions. Types are coarse.
agent_relevance: Reusable patterns concentrate in a few high-frequency families. Expect a heavy-tailed family structure in an agent's template library and store family-level templates first.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories
url: https://bura.brunel.ac.uk/handle/2438/1343 (author copy of Cognition 66:115-152; text opened from an author preprint)
finding: Statement of the original chunking theory and its machine form. Skill = a large indexed store of chunks reached by a discrimination net. Each chunk is also the condition of a production, so recognition evokes an action (a candidate move). Experts search forward from recognized patterns, novices work backward.
numbers: Parameters: STM about 7 chunks; one test in the net 10 ms; learning a new chunk about 8 s; 10 years or more of practice; 10,000 to 100,000 chunks (50,000 often quoted). MAPP (Simon & Gilmartin 1973) simulated a Class A player: below masters, above Class A recall.
limits: Review by an author of the successor theory, so partial toward templates. MAPP's own numbers were not opened here.
agent_relevance: Direct design source: recognition conditions that fire stored actions, found through a cheap index. This is the 'pattern cues candidate moves' mechanism in its simplest form.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories
url: https://bura.brunel.ac.uk/handle/2438/1343 (author copy of Cognition 66:115-152; text opened from an author preprint)
finding: Chase and Simon also proposed the mind's eye: chunks are activated by the board and trigger potential moves that are placed in STM for further examination. The choice of move then depends on selective search plus pattern recognition. De Groot's earlier finding: masters do not search deeper or wider; they find the right moves earlier.
numbers: De Groot: grandmaster about 93% correct after 2-5 s; weakest subject (class A level) about 50%. Masters seldom look at more than 100 continuations (De Groot 1978).
limits: A model claim described in a review, not a direct test. Direct tests of the recognition-to-move link are thin (see a27, a32).
agent_relevance: Core design claim: recognition proposes a short candidate list, search then checks it. This matches our rule that code checks and memory only proposes.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Experiment 1 of the template paper: recall of several boards in a row, which a pure STM chunk store cannot do. 13 players saw 1 to 5 game positions, 5 s each with 5 s gaps, then rebuilt all of them.
numbers: 13 players: 3 Masters (mean Elo 2453), 4 Experts (2180), 6 Class A (1883). 26 game positions (about 25 pieces, quiet, about move 20, obscure master games); three random positions as control. Trials: five with 1 board, three with 2, two with 3, one with 4, one with 5.
limits: Fixed order of rising difficulty (fatigue confound), partly answered by Exp 3. Mouse reconstruction slowed placement. Small N.
agent_relevance: A clean test of whether an expert store holds many items at once. Analogue for the agent: hold several partial tasks via compact pointers to templates instead of full text.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Results of Exp 1. The share of pieces right fell with more boards, but the number right rose well past what 7 chunks of 4-5 pieces (about 35 pieces) allow. Masters rebuilt up to 60 pieces, Experts about 40, Class A about 20. Chunks were bigger than the 1973 estimate and shrank when several boards were shown.
numbers: Random positions: Masters 21%, Experts 16%, Class A 12% (ns, F(2,10)=3.46). First-piece latency, one board: 3.1 s Masters, 3.6 Experts, 2.8 Class A; several boards: 6.0, 5.0, 3.9 s. Masters and Experts placed 2.3 chunks (1 board) rising to 9.9 (5 boards); some players placed 13 and 15 chunks. Largest chunk 19.7 pieces (Masters, 1 board) vs 12.4 (several); Experts 17 vs 9.8. Time on task vs score r=.94 (1 board), .74 (5 boards). U-shaped serial position for 4 boards: 40.8, 29.5, 20.7, 38.2%.
limits: Largest-chunk sizes depend on the 2 s rule applied to mouse input. The U-curve was not significant for 4 boards. Cooke et al. (1993) report a 2515-rated player holding 7 of 9 boards.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that experts do not store raw items; they hold a few pointers into large structures. Supports a memory with few large templates plus a short pointer list.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Experiment 2: more time between boards helped recall a lot, since slots can be filled and LTM learning can occur in the gap.
numbers: N=5 (1 GM 2575, 1 IM 2410, 1 Master 2280, 2 Experts 2050 and 2098). 2 or 4 boards, 5 s each, gaps 1, 2, 5, 10 s. Gain from 1 s to 10 s gap: Masters +71% (2 boards), +63% (4 boards); Experts +40%, +33%. At 10 s gap with 4 boards (100 pieces): Masters 82.9 pieces, Experts 44.9. Single board: Masters 92.3% right, Experts 64.5%; random: 21.1% and 17.7%.
limits: N=5. The 2 s and 5 s gaps gave no clear difference. A GM error (recalling the previous trial's board) lowered one cell. No pooled serial-position effect (50.5, 48.3, 51.1, 47.6%).
agent_relevance: Time to bind new material into an existing structure matters. A scaffold step that slots new facts into a template (rather than rewriting memory) matches this.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Experiment 3: one trained Master (the first author, Elo 2380) learned to recall many boards with a prelearned cue list (names of world champions), one position per name. Boards rose from 4 to about 9 and pieces right from about 50 to over 160. He still plateaued near the 7 plus-or-minus 2 board limit.
numbers: 150 sessions, one per day. Baseline without cue list: 50% and 55% (4 boards), 54.3% (5 boards); 79.9% on 2 boards. 8 s per board, 2 s gap. Adaptive rule: add a board if at most one board was below 60%. Peak block 152 pieces; later plateau about 123 pieces per block. Best sessions: 163 (9 boards), 160 (10), 167 (9), 178 (9) pieces.
limits: N=1 and the subject is an author. Part of the gain may be regained chess knowledge (percent per position also rose). One cue list only.
agent_relevance: Two layers matter: a deliberate index (cue list) that points to one template per item, and the templates themselves. An explicit index of solved cases keyed by short labels is the agent equivalent of the cue list.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Template theory. Some frequent chunks grow into templates. A template has a stable core (about a dozen pieces) and slots for variable information (piece, square, opening, plan, move) with default values, and links to other templates. Slots fill in under 1 s. Multiple templates (one per board) beat a single retrieval structure holding one board.
numbers: Core: 'perhaps a dozen pieces'. About 50,000 chunks or more in LTM. New chunk about 8 s (building the net); filling a slot on an existing node under 1 s. Prediction: at most 7 plus-or-minus 2 positions held, since one pointer per board sits in STM.
quote: chunks ... in long-term memory that contain variables (slots) and that these slots can be filled rapidly with new perceptual information
limits: Post-hoc fit to Exps 1-3 plus older data. The single-retrieval-structure version failed on four counts (location data, random positions predicted too well, one piece per square, too little interference). Core size and slot counts were not measured directly.
agent_relevance: The template is the most direct analogue of a solution template for our agent: fixed skeleton plus typed slots with defaults, linked to other templates. It also gives a cost model: building a new template is slow, filling a slot is fast.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: The paper reworked older anomalies. Charness (1976): a 30 s delay with interference cut recall only 6-8%. Frey & Adesman (1976): two boards, 8 s each, about 10 pieces per board. Chunk theory fits Frey and Adesman by arithmetic (two 3-piece chunks stored in LTM in 16 s plus 7 STM slots of 2 pieces gives about 20 pieces) but not Charness. Visuospatial interference cut recall by over two thirds, a verbal task did little (Bradley et al. 1987).
numbers: Charness: 6-8% loss. Learning time per chunk 5-10 s (Newell & Simon 1972). Saariluoma (1989): grandmasters encode up to 4 positions at 2 s per piece.
limits: Figures from other authors' studies, reported here, not re-opened. Depth-of-processing results (Goldin 1978; Frey & Adesman 1976) are confounded with presentation time.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'deeper' processing may be an artifact of more time. When we compare memory designs, equalize time and tokens spent.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted positions: implications for the theory of expertise
finding: Computer test of a simplified CHREST: do chunks include location? Fifty new positions in four versions (normal, flipped top-bottom, flipped left-right, rotated 180 degrees). The model learned from several thousand grandmaster positions, up to 70,000 nodes, with 20 random fixations per position.
numbers: Mean recall: normal 65.4%, horizontal 63.2%, vertical 53.3%, central 52.5%. Normal+horizontal minus vertical+central = 11.4 points. Recall = a + b log(nodes) explains over 98% of variance. Random positions rose slightly with nodes, up to 23.4%. The gap grew until about 2500 nodes, then stayed.
limits: Simplified model; learned and tested on the same kind of database.
agent_relevance: A runnable model shows that location-bound chunks give graded loss on transformed input and slow, log-like gain with store size. Use as a predicted curve for library-size experiments.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted positions: implications for the theory of expertise
finding: Human test, 25 players. Mirror-image distortions cost about 10 points of recall but did not drop it to random level. Chunks encode where pieces are, not only how they relate. This argues against Holding's claim that about 2,500 location-free schemas would do.
numbers: N=25: Masters n=5 (Elo 2395), Experts n=11 (2146), Class A n=9 (1890). Normal+horizontal: Masters 77.3%, Experts 49.7%, Class A 34.5%. Vertical+central: 62.9%, 38.6%, 27.5%. Gap 10.3 points (simulation 11.4). Skill F(2,22)=24.52; type F(3,66)=20.85; interaction F(6,66)=2.41, p<.05. Mean largest chunk: Masters 10.1, Experts 7.1, Class A 6.1; chunks per position 3.8, 4.1, 2.3. Chunk number change not significant.
limits: Reflection also changes the direction of relations, so part of the effect could be orientation-bound schemas. The authors say specific and general encodings may coexist. Two sites, slightly different materials.
agent_relevance: Specific patterns transfer less to transformed cases. If templates are stored in surface form, expect a drop on rephrased problems; test with paraphrase and symmetry controls.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted positions: implications for the theory of expertise
finding: Game vs random positions in the same 25 players. Chunk size and number collapse on random boards, and skill differences in chunk size appear only for game positions.
numbers: Largest chunk, game: 11.2 (Masters), 7.4 (Experts), 6.2 (Class A); random: 4.1, 4.3, 4.1. Chunks per position, game: 4.0, 4.3, 2.5; random: 1.2, 1.7, 1.8. Omission errors on random boards: 19.0, 16.1, 17.9. Commission errors: 2.4, 5.5, 3.9. Game vs random F(1,22)=291.51; skill x type F(2,22)=16.50, p<.001. Skill effect within random: F(2,22)=0.18, ns.
limits: Chunks include guessed and wrong pieces. Experts made more commission errors than Masters and Class A (inverted U).
agent_relevance: Template benefit depends on the input matching the learned distribution. The agent should detect that no template matches and fall back to generic search rather than force a template.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of rapidly presented random chess positions is a function of skill
finding: Review of random-position studies. The textbook claim that experts lose all advantage on random boards is wrong: across 13 comparisons the strongest group beat the weakest in 12. The gain is small (about one piece per 400 Elo vs about five pieces for game positions) and is not explained by better guessing.
numbers: Studies with 3 to 10 s exposure, at least 20 pieces, truly random. Strongest > weakest in 12 of 13 (binomial p=.0017). Randomized-block ANOVA, skill F(3,17)=10.35, p<.001. Masters average 5.5 pieces vs 2.6 for the weakest players. Commission errors at 5 s: Masters 1.0, Experts 3.1, Class A 3.4. Chase & Simon 1973 was the one exception (master below novice).
limits: Single studies mostly not significant (small N, small effect). Test statistics mostly unreported, so no pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: A correction of a famous null by low power. Template memory should give a small gain even off-distribution (accidental matches); we can test that prediction.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory
finding: Presentation time from 1 to 60 s. A Master at 1 s was about as good as Experts at 10 s. Masters hit a ceiling near 3 s. Recall follows 100 - B e^(-c(t-1)); both the share learned in the first second and the later rate rise with skill: stronger players see more at once and keep learning faster.
numbers: N=20: Masters n=5 (mean Elo 2498), Experts n=8 (2121), Class A n=7 (1879); one dropout. 19 game and 10 random positions; times 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 20, 30, 60 s. Game: rate c is 2x from Class A to Experts and 15x to Masters; first-second share (100-B) 1.3x and nearly 3x. Masters at 10 s: 92.4% mean; best-three fit B=24.56, c=0.72. Skill test at 10 s or less: F(2,16)=27.63, p<.001.
limits: Masters were not tested above 10 s on game positions. The fit for Masters is poorer (r2 .54 for the best three).
agent_relevance: Gives a timing law: part of the benefit is in the first look (recognition) and part in the rate of binding. Measure the first-pass benefit of a template separately from its benefit over many steps.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory
finding: Chunk numbers over time. Masters held few chunks: 2.9 at 1 s, 4.2 at 4 s, 3.3 at 10 s. Their largest chunk was already large at 1 s. Class A players kept adding chunks with time.
numbers: Masters 2.9 (1 s), 4.2 (4 s), 3.3 (10 s). Experts 2.2 (1 s), 4.5 (10 s), 2.9 (60 s). Class A 2.2 (1 s) rising to 5.4 (60 s). Largest chunk: Experts 9-10 pieces at start rising to about 17 at 60 s; Class A 4-5 pieces. Chunk number did not differ by skill at 10 s or less, F(2,16)=0.40, ns.
limits: Chunk number falls at long times because chunks merge. Uses the 2 s rule on mouse input.
agent_relevance: The big difference is the size of the unit, not how many units. Design for fewer, larger retrievable units.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory
finding: CHREST as a full implementation of template theory. Parts: LTM, discrimination net, a visual STM of three chunks, a mind's eye, an eye-movement module. Costs: new net node 8 s, adding to an existing chunk 2 s, filling a template slot 250 ms. It matches human recall curves for three net sizes.
numbers: STM = 3 visual chunks (from Zhang & Simon 1985, Richman et al. 1995). Visual field = squares within 2 of the fixated one. Nets of 500, 10,000 and 300,000 nodes chosen to match Class A, Expert and Master 5 s recall. Test on 50 game and 50 random positions unused in learning. All r2 of logistic fits above .95; the model underestimates human masters on game positions.
limits: Net size was fit to the 5 s data (two degrees of freedom spent per net). Parameters partly borrowed from verbal learning work. The model learns piece-position chunks only, not threats or plans.
agent_relevance: A worked example of fitting a library-size dial (500 / 10k / 300k nodes) to skill levels. We can sweep the number of stored templates the same way and read off a recall-vs-size curve.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory
finding: Random positions across presentation time. Skill differences were significant at short and at long times, and larger at long times. The learning-rate gap between game and random positions is huge for Masters.
numbers: Random: skill effect at 10 s or less F(2,15)=7.74, p<.005; above 10 s F(2,16)=14.36, p<.001. Rate c, game vs random: about 6x (Experts, Class A) and about 25x (Masters). First-second share (100-B), game vs random: about 2x (Experts, Class A) and about 3.5x (Masters).
limits: Small groups; parameter ratios have wide intervals. Random positions drawn from game piece sets.
agent_relevance: Large knowledge gives a big edge in-distribution and a small edge elsewhere. Report both when testing our template memory.

source: Gobet & Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory: evidence for the magical number four... or is it two?
finding: A test that separates chunking from template theory on chunk number and size. With a computer display, no more than about three chunks were recalled, and Masters placed chunks up to 15 pieces, as templates predict. The original 4-5 piece chunk size looks too small and the 7-chunk STM too large.
numbers: N=12: 4 Masters (mean BCF 202), 4 Class B (143), 4 novices. Copy and recall tasks, physical boards and computer display. Recall, game positions: 70.0% (Masters), 45.0% (Class B), 17.0% (novices); random: 22.3%, 16.9%, 14.4%. Median largest chunk, Masters, game: computer 14.8 (recall) and 12.9 (copy); physical board 7.5 and 3.8. Class B 9.0 and novices 6.3 (recall, computer). Chunks recalled on computer under 3; on physical boards up to 4.8. Skill F(2,9)=325.40; position type F(1,9)=64.72.
limits: Only 4 per cell. Chunk counts of 3 vs 7 depend on the 2 s rule and the apparatus (hand span breaks large chunks on physical boards). Authors say Cowan's figure of 4 may be too high.
agent_relevance: Argues for a small working list of large units. For an LLM scaffold, think of a short working list of big structured units rather than a long list of fragments.

source: Gobet & Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory: evidence for the magical number four... or is it two?
finding: Validation of the 2 s chunk boundary, by apparatus. Within-glance gaps are short and between-glance gaps long, but the computer display shifts the numbers up and so shifts chunk estimates.
numbers: Physical board: within-glance gaps mean 0.64 s (median 0.44), between-glance mean 2.43 s (median 2.20); 95% of within-glance gaps below 2 s vs 42.6% of between-glance. Computer: within 1.20 s (median 1.03), between 10.06 s (median 8.20). Chase & Simon: median within 1.00 s, mean between 3.00 s. Single pieces on random computer trials: 21 of 194, only 6 correct (28.6%).
limits: Younger participants than Chase & Simon, probably faster. Between-glance times on physical boards include parallel actions.
agent_relevance: A chunk metric depends on the measuring interface. Tie the agent's chunk metric to content (shared relations), not only to timing.

source: Gobet (1993) A computer model of chess memory
finding: First CHREST paper. It adds to MAPP a dynamic STM, recursive chunking, better perceptual mechanisms and a retrieval structure (a long-term template into which new information is encoded fast). It simulates three experiments: random vs game recall, several boards, mirror-image positions.
numbers: Reported fits include 97.4% of the Class A results in one experiment and 77.5% in another. Other fits quoted: 89.2% and 93.7% (the text does not make clear which cell each belongs to).
limits: The paper itself says some empirical phenomena are not captured and the link between representation and retrieval structure needs refinement. This version was later replaced by multiple templates.
agent_relevance: Shows how the model grew: each failed phenomenon forced a new mechanism. Our schema should likewise state what each memory part is for.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited
finding: Replication of de Groot's think-aloud study (position A) with 48 Swiss players. Total search size did not differ by skill, but depth and selectivity did. Masters looked at fewer base moves, had a shorter orientation phase and chose better moves. This supports 'recognition prunes the candidate set' but not 'masters search the same depth'.
numbers: N=48, 12 per level: Masters (mean Elo 2317), Experts (2101), Class A (1903), Class B (1699). Nodes: 58.0, 58.3, 56.8, 33.9 (ns). Base moves: Masters 3.2 vs Class A 6.5 (F(3,44)=2.94, p<.05). First phase: 1.1, 2.3, 1.6, 4.2 min (F=4.22, p=.01). Mean depth 5.0, 4.6, 3.7, 2.9 plies (0.6 ply per 200 Elo; Charness 1981: 0.5). Maximal depth 9.1 vs 8 plies, ns. Elo explains 29.2% of move-quality variance; 17.6% remains after search variables are partialled out.
limits: One position. These Masters were about 100 Elo below de Groot's. A 1986 secondary analysis with a controllability manipulation pooled. Elo explains only 29% of move quality, so the measure is noisy.
agent_relevance: Knowledge cut the candidate set (3.2 vs 6.5 base moves) without cutting total search. A scaffold can track candidate-set size and orientation time as signs that a template fired.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited
finding: Proposal for how templates tie search and recognition together. Patterns of pieces can be linked to moves and to move sequences, which makes search both more selective and deeper. Templates also carry evaluations that cut search. Search first rises with skill, then falls.
numbers: Elo explains 72.3% of recall variance (Gobet & Simon 1996, 25 players, Elo 1680-2590) but 29.2% of move quality. Reported from Saariluoma (1990): Masters (about 2200) 52 nodes at 5.1 depth vs IM and GM 23 nodes at 3.6.
limits: A theoretical proposal ('the theory postulates'), not tested in this paper. Links between templates as macro-operators are a conjecture.
agent_relevance: The clearest statement of the mechanism we want: pattern-to-move associations and links between templates as macro-operators. Treat as a hypothesis to test, not a result.

source: Gobet (2003) Forward search, pattern recognition and visualization in expert chess: a reply to Chabris and Hearst
finding: A dispute: is expert chess mostly recognition or mostly search? Chabris & Hearst (2003, Monaco tournament data) found more blunders in rapid and blindfold games than in classical games; Gobet replies that their results do not contradict the primacy of recognition and that both processes are already in templates and his SEARCH model.
numbers: Blunders per 1,000 moves as reported: rapid 6.85, blindfold 7.63, classical 5.02. Kasparov simultaneous-play results: median 2682 Elo, interquartile range 203.5 (with four added matches).
limits: The Chabris & Hearst paper itself was not opened, only Gobet's account. The classical vs rapid difference is small in absolute terms. Both sides agree that search and recognition both matter.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: pattern memory alone is not enough. Keep a checking or search step after the template proposes (our G3).

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories
url: https://bura.brunel.ac.uk/handle/2438/1343 (author copy of Cognition 66:115-152; text opened from an author preprint)
finding: Comparison of four theories on chess memory. Chunking and template theory predict a small expert edge on random boards; SEEK (Holding) predicts none; long-term working memory (square version) predicts a very large edge. Data favoured templates, then chunking. The square version would need about 160 ms to encode each piece.
numbers: 5 s / 32 pieces is about 160 ms per piece, vs at least 1 s per unit in other expertise tasks. Random boards: Masters 5.5 pieces vs weakest 2.6. Gobet & Simon 1995: Masters about 70% of pieces after 1 s and about 90% after 2 s. Ellis (1973): class A 6.7 of 8 pieces vs class D and below 4.5, at 150 ms.
limits: The author backs template theory. Ellis and Gobet & Simon 1995 are reported, not re-opened. The paper's fit table is qualitative.
agent_relevance: Competing explanations are listed with risky predictions. For our own design choices, write down what each rival predicts and test where they split.

source: Saariluoma (1991) blindfold dictated games; as reported in Gobet (1998)
url: https://bura.brunel.ac.uk/handle/2438/1343 (author copy of Cognition 66:115-152; text opened from an author preprint)
finding: Moves dictated at 2 s per piece moved. Masters located pieces almost perfectly after 15 moves of actual and random-legal games, but under 20% after random-illegal games. Chunk recognition fails when positions drift off the legal manifold.
numbers: Random-legal games about 60% after 25 moves vs actual games near 90%. Random-illegal games under 20% (as reported).
limits: Second-hand figures from Gobet (1998). Not opened.
agent_relevance: A clean off-distribution control: break the structure of inputs and the template advantage should vanish. Good test that a template store does real work.

source: Saariluoma (1994) quadrant swaps; as reported in Gobet & Simon (1996) and Gobet (1998)
finding: Swapping two board quadrants made the moved pieces hard to recall (worse than random), while unmoved quadrants stayed well recalled. Hybrid boards built from quadrants of four different games, kept in place, were recalled about as well as real games. So chunks carry location and a whole-position description is not needed.
numbers: No figures beyond 'dramatically reduced' for moved pieces and 'about as well as game positions' for hybrids (as reported). Subjects Class C to Expert.
limits: Second-hand. Some constructed positions are illegal. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Local patterns in the right place help even when the global gist is wrong. Argues for storing sub-templates that can be mixed, not only whole-problem templates.

source: Gobet & Jansen (1994) CHUMP, a chess program based on a model of human memory; via a Chess Programming Wiki summary seen in search results
finding: The main machine test of 'pattern cues move' in this literature. CHUMP learned piece patterns and the moves that followed them using CHREST's net, and proposed moves from recognized patterns. Its proposed moves matched actual moves better after learning in all test sets (Tal games, KQKR positions).
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Known only from a search snippet of a secondary summary, not the paper. Needs a follow-up read.
agent_relevance: The closest model of a pattern memory cueing candidate moves with a measured gain from learning. Priority read for the transfer angle.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Roles of recognition processes and look-ahead search in time-constrained expert problem solving (Kasparov simultaneous games); via search snippet and Gobet (2003)
finding: Performance argument: a top grandmaster playing several opponents at once lost only a little strength compared with tournament play, so recognition and not look-ahead carries much of high-level play.
numbers: Kasparov simultaneous play: median 2682 Elo, interquartile range 203.5 (from Gobet 2003 footnote).
limits: Abstract known only through a search snippet. Chabris & Hearst criticized the lack of variability data; the updated figures come from Gobet's reply.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that stored patterns can replace computation when time is short. In our budget scheme a template hit could justify a smaller token budget for that step.

source: Cross-domain replications of the expert-recall effect; as reported in Gobet (1998) and Gobet & Simon (1996)
url: https://bura.brunel.ac.uk/handle/2438/1343 (author copy of Cognition 66:115-152; text opened from an author preprint)
finding: The expert edge for meaningful over random material has been found in Go, gomoku, bridge, music, electronics circuits, computer programs and basketball. Some domains (music pitch symbols, dance sequences) show an expert edge even with random material.
numbers: Authors cited: Reitman 1976 (Go), Eisenstadt & Kareev 1977, Engle & Bukstel 1978 and Charness 1979 (bridge), Sloboda 1976 (music), Egan & Schwartz 1979 (electronics), McKeithen et al. 1981 (programming), Allard et al. 1980 (basketball).
limits: A list taken from reviews; presentation times varied too much for quantitative comparison. No LLM-agent measurement here.
agent_relevance: Some support that the finding is not chess-specific, so a template effect might appear for code or maths problems. Not shown for LLM agents in this angle.
